description: Curated synthetic educational examples for the Sprott-inspired Explorer. These codes are generated for Chaos Toolbox pedagogy and are not copied from historical Sprott dictionaries.
reference: Inspired by Julien C. Sprott, Strange Attractors: Creating Patterns in Chaos, M&T Books, 1993. Original Sprott dictionaries and figures are not redistributed here.

examples.name: Quadratic 1D map: read the orbit first
examples.notes: This is intentionally simple. It teaches how a compact code becomes an iterated orbit before moving to higher-dimensional images.
examples.learning_goal: Understand that a Sprott-style code is first a deterministic rule, not a finished picture.
examples.visual_intent: Shows x(n) against n with axes and grid so the learner sees transients, repeats, and low-complexity behavior.

examples.name: Henon-like map: first polished image
examples.notes: A compact synthetic 2D polynomial map that gives a recognizable folded attractor quickly.
examples.learning_goal: Start with a reliable attractive example before editing parameters or searching random codes.
examples.visual_intent: Uses high-density small points and time color to make the fold readable without axes.

examples.name: Henon-like map: bands reveal structure
examples.notes: Same equation as the first polished image, but the visual encoding changes the reading of the attractor.
examples.learning_goal: Learn that the same orbit can support different explanations depending on projection and color encoding.
examples.visual_intent: Shows quantized radius color as bands so invariant layers and density changes are easier to discuss.

examples.name: 3D map: color by depth
examples.equations: 3D quadratic polynomial map generated by Chaos Toolbox; use Codigos > Decodificar to inspect all coefficients.
examples.notes: This generated 3D map has a compact bounded cloud whose x-y projection is more legible when z is used as color.
examples.learning_goal: Use color to encode the hidden coordinate that is lost in a 2D projection.
examples.visual_intent: Projects x-y and colors by z so crossings in the plane become separated by depth.

examples.name: 3D map: compare another projection
examples.equations: 3D quadratic polynomial map generated by Chaos Toolbox; use Codigos > Decodificar to inspect all coefficients.
examples.notes: The equation is unchanged from the depth-color example. Only the projection changes.
examples.learning_goal: Compare projections before deciding whether an orbit is visually uninteresting.
examples.visual_intent: Uses x-z with z color to show that changing the plane can expose lobes hidden in x-y.

examples.name: 3D map: polished high-density image
examples.equations: 3D quadratic polynomial map generated by Chaos Toolbox; use Codigos > Decodificar to inspect all coefficients.
examples.notes: This is the improved version of the sparse-picture lesson: many points, small markers, and low opacity.
examples.learning_goal: Start with a rich image that also demonstrates how sample count and alpha improve a weak quick plot.
examples.visual_intent: Uses high-density time coloring to make layered returns visible on a dark background.

examples.name: 3D map: before visual improvement
examples.equations: 3D quadratic polynomial map generated by Chaos Toolbox; use Codigos > Decodificar to inspect all coefficients.
examples.notes: Same equation as the polished high-density example, but with too few points and a didactic white-background style.
examples.learning_goal: Learn why a quick sparse orbit can look poor even when the underlying code is useful.
examples.visual_intent: Shows the intentionally weak first render so the learner can compare it with the improved high-density version.

examples.name: 4D map: projected with w color
examples.equations: 4D quadratic polynomial map generated by Chaos Toolbox; use Codigos > Decodificar to inspect all coefficients.
examples.notes: Four-dimensional maps cannot be inspected directly, so the fourth coordinate is kept as color.
examples.learning_goal: Treat a 4D orbit as a projection problem rather than a single definitive plot.
examples.visual_intent: Projects x-y and colors by w to keep the lost fourth coordinate visible.

examples.name: 4D map: w bands
examples.equations: 4D quadratic polynomial map generated by Chaos Toolbox; use Codigos > Decodificar to inspect all coefficients.
examples.notes: This is the same 4D orbit as the previous example, rendered with discrete bands.
examples.learning_goal: Use banded color when continuous gradients hide ordering or layers.
examples.visual_intent: Quantizes w into bands so the 4D projection reads as layered structure.

examples.name: Five-term 3D flow: RK4 classroom render
examples.equations: dx/dt = y*z; dy/dt = x - y; dz/dt = 1 - x*y
examples.notes: This five-term flow is included as an educational equation example and rendered with a modern RK4 integrator.
examples.learning_goal: Compare map examples with continuous-time integration and a phase-space curve.
examples.visual_intent: Uses a 3D projection and z color so the continuous trajectory reads as a spatial object.

examples.name: Five-term 3D flow: Euler comparison
examples.equations: dx/dt = y*z; dy/dt = x - y; dz/dt = 1 - x*y
examples.notes: Euler is useful for discussing historical and numerical context, but RK4 is the safer default for polished images.
examples.learning_goal: See that the integration method is part of the visual result for flows.
examples.visual_intent: Uses a sober white-background x-y projection with axes so numerical-method differences are easier to compare.

examples.name: Generated 3D flow: depth and shadow
examples.equations: 3D quadratic flow generated by Chaos Toolbox; use Codigos > Decodificar to inspect all coefficients.
examples.notes: A generated flow with broad ranges. It is useful for teaching why flows usually need longer runs than maps.
examples.learning_goal: Tune color and density on a generated flow without relying on a famous named system.
examples.visual_intent: Uses radius color on a dark background to create depth cues and highlight the outer turns.

examples.name: Poor example: fixed orbit
examples.notes: A fixed orbit is useful because it shows why an arbitrary code is not automatically an attractor worth plotting.
examples.learning_goal: Recognize fixed-point collapse and avoid mistaking it for a failed renderer.
examples.visual_intent: Shows a flat time series with axes: the visual failure is the mathematical behavior.

examples.name: Poor example: divergent orbit
examples.notes: This orbit grows until it crosses the divergence threshold. It is included to teach the warning state.
examples.learning_goal: Understand that divergence is a valid search outcome and should trigger a parameter or code change.
examples.visual_intent: Uses a didactic time projection so the learner sees why the plot cannot become a bounded attractor.
